chunks: From him, from Ahmad ibn Idris, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from Salih ibn Razin, from Ibn Ashyam, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him).

Regarding a slave owned by a group of people who were permitted for him to trade: a man gave him one thousand dirhams and said to him, 'Buy a person with it, free him, and perform Hajj on his behalf with the remainder.' The owner of the one thousand dirhams died, so the slave went and bought his father, freed him on behalf of the deceased, and gave the remainder to him to perform Hajj on behalf of the deceased. This reached the masters of his father, his own masters, and the heirs of the deceased, and they all disputed over the one thousand dirhams. The masters of the manumitter said, 'You bought your father from our wealth,' and the masters of the slave said, 'You bought your father with our wealth.'

Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said: 'As for the Hajj, it has proceeded with what is in it. As for the freed man, he returns to slavery for the masters of his father. Whichever of the two parties establishes proof that he bought his father with their wealth, he has slavery over him.'

key_terms.عَبْدٌ لِقَوْمٍ: A slave owned by a group of people
key_terms.مَأْذُونٌ لَهُ فِي التِّجَارَةِ: Permitted to trade (manumission with commercial rights)

ai.seo_question: How is the ownership of a slave determined when he uses entrusted funds to buy and free his father?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* illustrates the Shia juristic principle of tracing property rights through evidentiary proof (*bayyina*) in cases of mixed ownership. Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies that while the Hajj obligation is fulfilled regardless of the dispute, the slave's reversion to slavery is contingent upon which party successfully proves their financial contribution to the purchase. This ruling underscores the importance of clear documentation in commercial transactions involving emancipation (*itq*) within the framework of *fiqh al-jafari*.
